title: Telegram Serverless

sections.title: The module system
sections.description: At runtime, a module can see exactly two things: the platform SDK and the other modules in your project. There are no npm packages, no filesystem, and no network except through the SDK's fetch.

sections.title: Handlers
sections.description: A handler is a module in handlers/ whose default export the platform invokes when a matching update arrives.

sections.title: Endpoints
sections.description: An endpoint is a module in endpoints/ that your Mini App calls — the place for anything the front‑end can't do on its own, like reading and writing the database, calling the Bot API, or talking to outside services with y

sections.title: What gets deployed
sections.description: When you npx tgcloud push, the CLI gathers every .js file under schema.js, lib/, handlers/, and endpoints/, and sends that exact set as your project's module space — together with the Mini App's build folder, if tgcloud.

sections.title: Mini App front-end

sections.title: The database
sections.description: Every bot gets its own database — an SQLite‑backed store that persists between invocations and is available to every module through db. You describe your tables in schema.js with a small, typed DSL; you read and write th

sections.title: Declaring tables
sections.description: Tables are named exports in schema.js. Calling table() builds a description at load time (it does not touch the database); the platform discovers the exported tables when you deploy schema.js and migrates the database to

sections.title: No foreign keys
sections.description: The runtime runs with PRAGMA foreign_keys off. A declared foreign key would be silently inert — no cascades, no orphan protection — which is worse than having none at all, so the DSL makes it impossible. Namely, .referen

sections.title: Querying
sections.description: db is a fluent query builder. Every query is asynchronous — the terminal methods (.all(), .get(), .values(), .run()) return Promises, so always await.

sections.title: Migrations
sections.description: Your database changes as your bot grows. The platform keeps that safe by separating deploying code from changing data, and by classifying every schema change by how risky it is.

sections.title: The SDK
sections.description: At runtime a module has one library: sdk. It bundles the three things a bot backend needs — a database, the Telegram Bot API, and outbound HTTP — with nothing to install and no credentials to configure. The database (db)

sections.title: The Bot API
sections.description: api gives you the entire Telegram Bot API. Call any method as api.<method>(params). Every current — and future — Bot API method works with no SDK update required.

sections.title: HTTP
sections.description: fetch is a fetch‑like client for calling the outside world — third‑party APIs, webhooks, anything over HTTP.

sections.title: Logging
sections.description: The standard global console is available — nothing to import, it's just there as in any JavaScript. Its output is captured and shown by npx tgcloud run, which makes it your primary debugging tool during development.

sections.title: Command-line interface
sections.description: tgcloud is the bridge between your project folder and the cloud. It scaffolds projects, shows you what changed, deploys, runs modules, and applies database migrations. It needs Node.js 18 or newer. Two ways to get it:

sections.title: Authentication
sections.description: A project is tied to one bot by its token, which has the form app<id>:<secret>. The app<id> part is public and may be printed; the secret never appears in logs or errors.
